items.question: Why do you see world models as a promising path to open-ended learning?
items.object: World models as a path to open-ended learning
items.answer: I decided to do a PhD where I focused on open-ended learning, reinforcement learning still, and then got a bit into world models. By the time I finished my PhD, I was increasingly convinced that the combination of these ideas would be the really powerful big thing to do. After my PhD, I joined Google DeepMind and worked a little bit on a project called Adaptive Agents, which was in the XLand environment. After that, pretty much started Genie. I've been doing that for a few years. I'm in the open-endedness team, which encompasses some other areas, too, but we've been focusing on this idea of using world models as a path to open-endedness as part of the Genie project.

items.question: Why did Ha and Schmidhuber’s 2018 World Models paper resonate with you?
items.object: Ha and Schmidhuber’s 2018 World Models paper
items.answer: For me, it was really the Ha and Schmidhuber work in 2018, around the time I was getting interested in this field, that really resonated. I was looking at reinforcement learning tasks. At the time these were MuJoCo tasks, like little half-cheetah ones. The World Models paper was basically saying that with a few offline examples, we could simulate an environment, predicting the next state sufficiently well that we could train policies in that model and then transfer them back to a real environment. The policy never trained in the real environment. Obviously, that's super cool. But the setting they had was basically that you had data from the real environment.
quotes: For me, it was really the Ha and Schmidhuber work in 2018, around the time I was getting interested in this field, that really resonated. I was looking at reinforcement learning tasks. The response notes that Ha and Schmidhuber’s World Models approach still required data from the real environment.

items.question: What do you see as the limitation of the earlier world-model research paradigm, where researchers already had access to the environment?
items.object: World models for environments researchers already had access to
items.answer: That was the paradigm that world models were in for a few years: it was showing that we could do this at all for increasingly complex environments where we actually had the environment. If we didn't want to do model-based reinforcement learning and use world models, we could have just used a distributed world algorithm and probably got really good performance a different way. There were still benefits to doing the world model approach. Maybe it was more sample-efficient, but it wasn't solving something you couldn't otherwise solve.
quotes: That was the paradigm that world models were in for a few years: it was showing that we could do this at all for increasingly complex environments where we actually had the environment. If we didn't want to do model-based reinforcement learning and use world models, we could have just used a distributed world algorithm and probably got really good performance a different way. There were still benefits to doing the world model approach. Maybe it was more sample-efficient, but it wasn't solving something you couldn't otherwise solve.

rubrics.text: The response states that, when researchers already had access to the environment, world models did not make otherwise unsolvable tasks solvable.

items.question: How did progress in text-to-image models shape your idea of a foundation world model?
items.object: Foundation world models
items.answer: I think we were both excited about that at the same time from different angles. For me, that was saying, "Look, if we can do text-to-image this well"—and I think it was maybe four years ago that Imagine came out—"then video will happen at some point. After video, maybe we'll be able to get to world models, and we'll be able to simulate anything with large data sets." The idea was, can we take the same concept and apply it to what I would view as a world model, which is simulating an environment, and therefore simulate any environment? That's why we came up with this idea of a foundation world model: a world model, but rather than just being for one single environment, it's any possible or new environment, like a foundation model.

items.question: How has your understanding of what counts as a world model changed as video models have entered the discussion?
items.object: The definition of a world model
items.answer: This was a hard line we stuck to: a foundation world model is this one thing. It predicts the next state given actions. But increasingly other kinds of models have been considered to be world models recently, for example video models, text-to-video. At first, that didn't really fit with how I saw world models, but actually I think it kind of does at a different level of abstraction. I think now I have a slightly broader view of a world model: models that simulate the future given the past and some form of actions, and simulate dynamics of a world. It's not explicitly modeling every transition of an MDP, which is what I would have said before, but maybe just simulating the dynamics of the world in some way that you can act and intervene in it and then get counterfactual information. That enables things like planning or learning policies in simulation.

items.question: How do you think about communicating the lack of real-time playability when announcing earlier Genie research?
items.object: Communicating the lack of real-time playability in earlier Genie research
items.answer: I definitely think we did try to emphasize it wasn't real-time in both your papers. The challenge was, if you're announcing a new piece of research, you're not going to say, "Welcome to our non-real-time breakthrough," because it's not the best way to make it sound exciting. You don't want to open with a limitation. But then if you put the limitation halfway down and you've got a bunch of cool videos, people don't really get that far. We definitely had this challenge. I will say it was slightly less than 20 minutes. I think it was more like 30 seconds.

items.question: How do you assess Genie 1's contribution as a proof of concept for foundation world models?
items.object: Genie 1 as a proof of concept for foundation world models
items.answer:
Essentially, Genie 1 was quite a different beast to Genie 3. It was really the first proof of concept of this foundation world model idea: a model that could generate new worlds. There'd obviously been amazing progress in world models for single domains, starting with the Atari suite of work and then things like Dreamer, DreamerV2, DreamerV3, that could model increasingly complex individual environments and show that you could use them for agents to learn amazing behaviors that could solve really complex tasks. That's really important work in one axis, which is single-domain complexity. Whereas Genie 1 was basically saying, "We don't care about the complexity of the environments per se. Can we train a model that can generate new environments and new worlds at all?"

For Genie 1, it was a quite new idea: could we do it at all? But it was limited in scope. We trained two models, which people don't really notice as well. We trained one model on this 2D platformer game data set, and another model on the robotics dataset from, I think, the RT-1 paper, which was this everyday robotics arm. In both cases, you could unsupervised-learn an action space that meant you could give the model a new image that wasn't in the training data. Maybe it was generated by a text-to-image model; maybe it was a photograph you took yourself. Then you could play it like a world using the latent actions. That sounds amazing, but there were caveats. It was 90p, so very small, and it lasted maybe a couple of seconds before it degraded. It didn't really generate anything new when you went off-screen. We used this masked-gate approach, and it tended to have mode collapse when you moved away. If you look at the platformer examples, when you move to the right, it just continued a flat platform rather than generating exciting new content. People did notice that, but we were definitely aware of it. It was more just, this is kind of cool that this remotely works. It was a very early-stage project. When we started, no one really thought it was worth doing. Luckily, we're in a place like Google DeepMind where people encourage these more exploratory projects, but it wasn't a heavily resourced effort. It was a few of us scrapping together.

items.question: How did you come to see latent action learning as a promising approach to building world models from unlabeled videos?
items.object: Latent action learning for world models trained on unlabeled videos
items.answer:
The challenge with that was on the data side because unlike training from existing environments, we don't have actual labeled data from your target environment if you're going to generate new things. So we collected a data set of unlabeled videos that had no action labels, and we had this neat approach where we learned latent actions. The nice thing about that was that it was an example of bumping into someone who had almost a perfect skill set for the thing I was excited about doing and the things I didn't know about. I've been fortunate about this a few times in my career. Ashley had worked on latent action learning for more than five years. She is one of the people who really pioneered that direction, but in a different context. She was working on it to learn behaviors from videos. You take videos and want to extract the actions so you can behavior-clone or do imitation learning from those videos; you need to learn unsupervised latent actions so you can do that. We had the opposite setup. Instead of trying to learn behaviors from the videos, we tried to learn a world model from the videos so that we could use the world model to learn policies. It's a different framing.

There had been a paper at CVPR called Playable Environments, which did a similar thing. It was Menapace et al. That came out as I was writing my PhD thesis, and I was thinking, how are we going to do these world models from internet videos? How are we going to make this possible? Then I saw that paper and thought, "Well, that's at least one path." I got chatting to Ashley, and she was thinking, "Well, actually that does make sense. We could definitely go for this approach, and it'd be a really exciting way of getting the latent actions to work at larger scale than she'd previously tried before."

items.question: Why did you consider Genie 2's move to larger-scale 3D world generation an exciting research result?
items.object: Scaling Genie 2 to generate 3D worlds
items.answer: We had the results for a while and had already started thinking about future plans. Around that time, there was a lot of progress on video models in general. They had their moment, like text-to-image a few years before. It became very clear to us that for the next phase of Genie, we could go for something a bit larger-scale, and it would probably work, because we'd seen that video models had scaled pretty effectively. We decided to go from 2D games to a dataset of any 3D world, and scaled it up to 360p. It had the ability to generate environments again from image prompts that lasted maybe 10, 20 seconds before they degraded. It wasn't real-time, but you could play with it for a couple of minutes and wait a few seconds for each frame. It kind of worked for 3D worlds. That was not completely obviously going to work, because it was doing autoregressive generation, and it still wasn't clear that this would last even 10, 20 seconds. I think it was quite an exciting result.

items.question: How do you assess Genie 2 as a step toward a more capable world model?
items.object: Genie 2's progress and limitations as a world model
items.answer:
Genie 2 was a diffusion model, so it had slightly different properties, but it still was only supporting image prompting. It wasn't anywhere near as expressive as video models. It still required you to select an image for it that worked, which didn't always work. It couldn't generate its own worlds. It required you to generate an image that was in a certain kind of format where there's a clear agent in the right location, for example, and then it would simulate from there. Whereas what I'm hoping we spend a lot of time talking about with Genie 3 is that it can definitely do that.

To bookend this part, Genie 2 at the time was a good sign of life for this general approach, but it wasn't real-time. We'd seen with Game Engine that it was really impactful if you get that right. The visual quality was good, but it still wasn't using text as input, wasn't as expressive, and it was nowhere near the visual quality of state-of-the-art video models like Veo 2, which came out the same time and was mind-blowing for all of us. That's where Genie 3 and Shlomi came in, and he had expertise. I like to borrow people's expertise, and at that point it was pretty clear we had an expert in those areas.

items.question: What makes Genie 3’s futuristic Tokyo office and jungle example your favorite demonstration of the model?
items.object: Genie 3’s futuristic Tokyo office and jungle example
items.answer: My favorite example is this one where you start in this futuristic Tokyo office, and you say, "I want to walk outside," and you turn around and go outside and you're in the jungle. The laptop is in the jungle too. Genie 3 knows that it updates both, which I think is pretty incredible. When you turn away, you see outside is actually the jungle, just as in the prompt. When you go into the jungle and turn back around, you see the office that they're in, and you see them playing. You kind of have to see it to believe it, but I think it quite incredibly represents how the model actually does have some understanding of things, because it understands that when it updates the screens, it should do both. It also understands that if you're in an office and you go outside and look back, then you should see some kind of building that they should be in. I think that's really cool. It's definitely not what the goal of the project was, to be able to do that. But sometimes when you pursue interesting objectives, unexpected things can arise. I think that's a really nice example.

items.question: What do you find significant about the Genie 3 demonstration where painted strokes remain intact after the view pans away and back?
items.object: Genie 3’s wall-painting demonstration
items.answer: When we saw that generated by someone, there was a bit of disbelief across some people in my team, because we didn't even know the model was capable of doing something like that. It's not just that the original visual world is maintained, but the actions you took in it and the consequences of the actions you took are maintained as well. It's also pretty cool because it shows you could use the model for more vocational things as well. I think that's quite interesting as a use case that we didn't really think of.

items.question: How do you think about the challenge of building Genie 3 to combine memory, high resolution, diversity of worlds, and real-time performance?
items.object: Genie 3’s development and combined capabilities
items.answer: We had to really set ourselves as a team this goal of trying to be ambitious in all these dimensions. If you don't commit to it right at the beginning, it'll be very hard to achieve all of it in one go, which is really the challenge and the magic of the model: it can have memory, high resolution, diversity of worlds, and also be real-time. In each of those dimensions, we had really amazing people in the team. From the acknowledgements, you can see it's a slightly bigger team than we obviously had before in the Genie series. I would consider it almost like a new model, but with inherited name. We had great people in all these different areas who worked really hard on each individual component, but also with awareness of the other parts. It's incredible to see the kind of things people were able to put together. Each one was a challenge. It wasn't the case that any one of those parts was easy to achieve.

items.question: What do you see as necessary for a world model to learn consistency without an explicit representation of the world?
items.object: Learning world consistency without explicit world representations
items.answer: Every part has to be really done carefully, because the model will learn what's in the data. You have to have a really capable model that can do that, but you also have to train it on the right data so that it does learn the right things. It has to be a lot of things coming together to get that without adding those other methods.

items.question: How do you see Genie 3 expanding what SIMA agents can learn in 3D worlds?
items.object: Genie 3 as a training environment for SIMA agents
items.answer:
We designed this to be an environment for agents. At Google DeepMind, obviously we have lots of projects working on agents, and the one that's really focused on 3D worlds is the SIMA agent. They're trying to train agents that can achieve language goals in 3D simulated environments. Right now, they're training in existing games. They've got a really capable agent that can do quite diverse things in different game worlds, but ultimately it's limited by only having access to those game worlds. It can't train in any imaginable game world or in the real world because it's got access to a finite set of environments to train in.

This is the exact problem Genie is trying to solve: to generate new environments. But the SIMA agent was surprisingly general. Even though it's been trained on a smaller set of worlds, you can drop it in one of the Genie environments that it's never seen before. You use text to create a Genie 3 environment or world, say you describe a scene that could be a factory floor, and in the background there's a forklift truck. You generate this world and say to the SIMA agent, "Go to the forklift truck," or even, "Go to the thing that can lift things." The SIMA agent from that point onwards treats the Genie-generated world as if it's any other environment. It doesn't know that it's a model; it doesn't know anything. It just sees the pixels and says, "I'm going to press this key to achieve this goal." All Genie sees is the key press. It doesn't know what the agent's trying to do, because if it did know that, it might make it happen. All it knows is it wants to go forward. Then it simulates the next frame, the SIMA agent sees the next frame, and says, "Okay, I'm going to keep going forward." They happen in tandem, back and forth.

Critically, if the SIMA agent does the wrong actions, it won't achieve the goal. If it does the right actions, it will achieve the goal. Then the SIMA agent can learn from this experience to achieve the goal more often. There may be some things it can't do yet but could learn to do in these worlds. We essentially have signs of life that one agent is interacting with another one, to teach it new skills in these more embodied worlds, at a scale that hasn't really been done before.

To close the loop on this, a really cool thing could be integrating this with the world events. Even a benign environment like walking down the street might become much more interesting if you injected, say, a cat jumps out or something like that. You can teach agents to be robust to all these different kinds of things, even in simple environments, because we have this additional lever to pull on the environment side to make it more interesting and challenging for the agents.
quotes: we designed this to be an environment for agents. At Google DeepMind, obviously we have lots of projects working on agents, and the one that's really focused on 3D worlds is the SIMA agent. They're trying to train agents that can achieve language goals in 3D simulated environments.

Right now, they're training in existing games. They've got a really capable agent that can do quite diverse things in different game worlds, but ultimately it's limited by only having access to those game worlds. It can't train in any imaginable game world or in the real world because it's got access to a finite set of environments to train in.

This is the exact problem Genie is trying to solve: to generate new environments. But the SIMA agent was surprisingly general. Even though it's been trained on a smaller set of worlds, you can drop it in one of the Genie environments that it's never seen before. You use text to create a Genie 3 environment or world, say you describe a scene that could be a factory floor, and in the background there's a forklift truck. You generate this world and say to the SIMA agent, "Go to the forklift truck," or even, "Go to the thing that can lift things." The SIMA agent from that point onwards treats the Genie-generated world as if it's any other environment. It doesn't know that it's a model; it doesn't know anything. It just sees the pixels and says, "I'm going to press this key to achieve this goal." All Genie sees is the key press. It doesn't know what the agent's trying to do, because if it did know that, it might make it happen. All it knows is it wants to go forward. Then it simulates the next frame, the SIMA agent sees the next frame, and says, "Okay, I'm going to keep going forward." They happen in tandem, back and forth.

Critically, if the SIMA agent does the wrong actions, it won't achieve the goal. If it does the right actions, it will achieve the goal. Then the SIMA agent can learn from this experience to achieve the goal more often. There may be some things it can't do yet but could learn to do in these worlds. We essentially have signs of life that one agent is interacting with another one, to teach it new skills in these more embodied worlds, at a scale that hasn't really been done before. items.question: How do you assess Genie 3’s ability to simulate interactions with other agents?
items.object: Genie 3’s simulation of other agents
items.answer: We mentioned that this is quite limited at this point. Ultimately the model is predicting the next frames. It's able to get some very basic simulation of other agents. If you walk in their way, if they're walking and you stand in the way, they might stop; or if a car is driving and you walk in front of it, it might stop. But it's not the case that this is very complex interaction. That's definitely a limitation. It's also something that's maybe much more advanced in video already. It's something that we don't have for sure.

items.question: How do you view Genie 3’s one-minute visual memory in the context of progress in your field?
items.object: Genie 3’s one-minute visual memory limitation
items.answer: I think there's clearly the one-minute limitation as well. It's kind of funny to say it because Genie 1 and 2, a minute would have been seen as incredible. But the pace of our field is absolutely crazy, so this is the kind of thing that will seem embarrassingly short in the future. Right now, we say we have visual memory for a minute.

items.question: How do you assess Genie 3’s ability to depict specific real-world locations compared with abstract worlds?
items.object: Genie 3’s accuracy in depicting real-world locations
items.answer: There is also real-world physical accuracy; it's not perfect. If you say, "I want my exact street in London," it doesn't know my street. Some elements of that could be improved. If in text you describe a very abstract world, it will almost certainly get it on the money. If you describe a specific geographic location, you might notice that it's not what you hoped it would be in some way. That's another limitation.

items.question: Why do you see models like Genie 3 as an exciting path toward teaching agents to interact with people in the physical world?
items.object: Genie 3 for teaching agents to interact with people in embodied worlds
items.answer: There are so many exciting ideas already mentioned. I think the one that really excites me is teaching agents to interact in visually realistic, embodied worlds with people in the worlds. I think that's a really missing capability for any of our current agents: to interact in the physical world with humans as well. Models like Genie 3 could enable that. I also don't really think there's any other way to achieve that. That's something really exciting, especially with the world events, which could enable generating diverse scenarios that we wouldn't be able to get data for any other way. I think this is still fairly early in the journey, but this is a big step that will open up a lot of use cases there.
